## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Macchajātaka* (Ja 34) is a story of the Buddha's previous life belonging to the *Ekanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Its canonical verse begins with the opening line *Na maṁ sītaṁ na maṁ uṇhaṁ* ("'Tis not the cold [nor heat that troubles me]") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. According to the narrative framework (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the tale while dwelling at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, addressing a monk who was discontented and overcome by longing for his former wife (*purāṇadutiyikā*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].
In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was born as a king's royal chaplain (*purohita*) [Fausböll 1877]. He encountered a male fish caught in a fisherman's net who lamented not his physical capture or suffering, but rather the fear that his female mate would believe he had abandoned her out of infatuation with another fish; moved by this, the chaplain secured the fish's release back into the water [Fausböll 1877]. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Buddha revealed the Four Noble Truths, leading the passion-tossed monk to the attainment of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and identified the births: the female fish was the former wife, the male fish was the monk, and the chaplain was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877].
Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora for this text, and DharmaNexus records no Pali-internal text reuse [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. The narrative is distinct from two other Pali Jātakas bearing the same name: the rainmaking *Macchajātaka* (Ja 75) and a later *Dukanipāta* story (Ja 216).
